Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- While many now recognize the scientific explanation for a solar eclipse, the phenomenon is still marked with tradition and sometimes suspicion in Hindu-majority India. People test the "sky watching telescope" at the Gujarat Council of Science City in India. The "exceptionally long" eclipse that will cross half the planet Wednesday will be able to be seen by virtually all of the population of China and India. For beggars in India, the occasion means an extra day of receiving alms and food. The panhandler in Sandeep Jaggi's neighborhood normally visits the block every week on Tuesdays and Saturdays, as well as the days of a new and full moon. And because his patrons mark an eclipse with alms-giving, prayers and bathing, he rarely misses the chance to meet them on this day as well. "It's a family tradition and I follow it," says 34-year-old Jaggi. He will fill the beggar's small steel pail with mustard oil and coins and his disheveled sash with lentils. For others in the country, the eclipse is not a reason to celebrate, but a more ominous phenomenon. Send us your photos of the eclipse . Most pregnant women hope to avoid giving birth during an eclipse. "None of the expectant mothers under my treatment are willing to have deliveries on Wednesday," Shivani Sachdev Gour, a gynecologist at New Delhi's Fortis La Femme hospital, told CNN. In fact, there are critically ill patients who do not want to be in the hospital on the day of the eclipse, she said. Indian astrologers even advise expectant mothers to stay indoors when this celestial event occurs. "It may not cause any physical harm to the baby, but it may affect the child's overall personality," said R.K. Sharma, who describes himself as a "remedial astrologer." A solar eclipse, he says, weakens the sun god temporarily because of an encounter with dragon Rahu and leaves some cascading results everywhere. "Bathing in holy rivers and ponds during this time thus helps protect health and develop positivism and greater will power," he explained. About 1.5 million people are expected at one such pond -- the Brahmsarovar, or the pool of Hindu god Brahma -- in northern India on Wednesday. "They offer prayers to the sun god and take holy dips during an eclipse," said Ashok Kumar Bansal, the sub-divisional magistrate of Kurukshetra, an ancient Hindu city. But the century's longest total solar eclipse is not just about the dragon-sun combat, it also means business for some. Travel firms in India have plans in place to cash in on the phenomenon. Cox and Kings India has a planeload of eclipse watchers heading for the eastern state of Bihar, one of the most preferred locations for sighting the event. The plane will hover over Gaya in Bihar and return to New Delhi the same day, company spokesman Thomas C. Thottathil told CNN. Passengers were given two options: to book a "sunside" seat facing the eclipse for about $1,640, or reserve an "earthside" seat for about $610, Thottathil added. "And it's a sold out flight now!" he said.

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) — Although the science behind solar eclipses is widely understood today, in Hindu-majority India the event continues to be associated with ritual, custom and, at times, apprehension.

At the Gujarat Council of Science City, visitors try out a “sky-watching telescope.” Wednesday’s “exceptionally long” eclipse will pass across half the globe and should be visible to nearly everyone in China and India.

For India’s beggars, an eclipse can bring an additional opportunity to receive food and donations. In Sandeep Jaggi’s neighborhood, a local panhandler usually makes his rounds every Tuesday and Saturday, as well as on new-moon and full-moon days. Because Jaggi and other benefactors observe eclipses by praying, bathing and giving alms, the beggar is also careful to visit on such occasions.

“It’s a family tradition and I follow it,” said Jaggi, 34. He plans to pour mustard oil and coins into the man’s small steel bucket and place lentils in his untidy sash.

Elsewhere in India, however, the eclipse is regarded less as a festive event than as a troubling sign. Readers are invited to submit their eclipse photographs.

Many pregnant women prefer not to deliver a baby during an eclipse. Shivani Sachdev Gour, a gynecologist at Fortis La Femme hospital in New Delhi, told CNN that none of the expectant mothers in her care wanted to give birth on Wednesday. She added that even some critically ill patients did not wish to remain in the hospital on the day of the eclipse.

Indian astrologers also recommend that pregnant women remain inside while the celestial event is taking place.

“It may not cause any physical harm to the baby, but it may affect the child’s overall personality,” said R.K. Sharma, who calls himself a “remedial astrologer.”

According to Sharma, a solar eclipse occurs when the sun god is temporarily diminished through an encounter with the dragon Rahu, producing a range of consequences.

He said that bathing in sacred rivers and ponds during the eclipse can therefore safeguard health while encouraging positivity and stronger willpower.

Around 1.5 million people are expected to gather Wednesday at one such body of water in northern India: Brahmsarovar, also known as the pool of the Hindu god Brahma.

“During an eclipse, they pray to the sun god and immerse themselves in the holy water,” said Ashok Kumar Bansal, sub-divisional magistrate of Kurukshetra, an ancient Hindu city.

Yet the century’s longest total solar eclipse is not solely associated with the mythical struggle between the dragon and the sun. For some, it is also a commercial opportunity.

Indian travel companies have organized special offerings designed to profit from the event. Cox and Kings India is flying a group of eclipse enthusiasts to Bihar in eastern India, considered one of the best places from which to view the phenomenon.

Company spokesman Thomas C. Thottathil told CNN that the aircraft would circle above Gaya, Bihar, before returning to New Delhi later that same day.

Travelers could choose between a “sunside” seat overlooking the eclipse for approximately $1,640 and an “earthside” seat costing about $610, Thottathil said.

“And it’s a sold-out flight now!” he added.

Some families mark an eclipse by praying, bathing, and giving alms to beggars, including food, oil, and coins. Astrologers may also advise people to take spiritual precautions, such as bathing in holy waters to guard against the eclipse’s perceived negative influence. outputs.L4:
As a major solar eclipse approaches, people across India respond with a striking mixture of scientific curiosity, religious devotion, and deep-rooted anxiety. Astronomers and educators explain the event as the predictable passage of the Moon between Earth and the Sun, while public institutions warn viewers to protect their eyes with approved filters. Yet for many Indians, an eclipse is not merely a celestial spectacle. It is also a spiritually charged period associated with danger, impurity, and powerful unseen forces.

Interviews with families, priests, doctors, and astrologers reveal how traditional beliefs continue to shape everyday decisions. Some people plan to fast during the eclipse, avoid cooking or eating, and discard food prepared before it begins. Others intend to remain indoors, close doors and curtains, chant prayers, or bathe once the eclipse has ended. Temples may alter their opening hours, while worshippers perform purification rituals and make donations to priests, beggars, or charitable institutions. Almsgiving is widely regarded as especially meritorious at such a moment, when ordinary cosmic and spiritual boundaries are believed to be disturbed.

Pregnant women are often subject to particular restrictions. In some households, they are advised not to go outside, handle sharp objects, sew, cut food, or expose themselves to the eclipsed Sun. Such precautions arise from the belief that an eclipse can harm an unborn child or cause physical abnormalities. Medical professionals generally reject these claims, emphasizing that eclipses do not pose a special danger to pregnancy beyond the risk of eye injury from looking directly at the Sun. Nevertheless, doctors may encounter patients who postpone appointments, procedures, or travel because relatives consider the timing inauspicious.

Astrology further reinforces the eclipse’s significance. Astrologers interpret it as an event capable of affecting individuals, governments, and society, with its consequences depending on zodiac signs, planetary positions, and the geographical path of the shadow. Some people consult astrologers to learn whether they should undertake special prayers, make donations, or delay important decisions. Even individuals who accept the scientific explanation may continue to observe these practices as a precaution or as an expression of family and cultural identity.

This coexistence of science and tradition is one of the most revealing aspects of India’s response. Many people understand perfectly well that an eclipse is caused by the alignment of the Sun, Moon, and Earth. They may also know when it will begin, how long it will last, and how to view it safely. Scientific knowledge, however, does not necessarily erase inherited customs. A person can recognize the astronomical mechanism while still fasting, praying, avoiding certain activities, or following the advice of elders.

The eclipse therefore becomes more than a rare event in the sky. It exposes the complicated ways in which modern education, medicine, religion, astrology, and family tradition interact. Rational understanding may have reduced some fears, especially among younger and urban populations, but it has not eliminated the sense that an eclipse is exceptional and potentially dangerous. Reverence and apprehension remain powerful, shaping behavior even among those who do not fully accept the beliefs behind the rituals.

Ultimately, India’s response demonstrates the enduring cultural power of eclipses. Scientific explanations can describe how they happen and public-health guidance can make viewing them safe, but neither automatically removes the meanings societies have attached to them over centuries. The eclipse remains both an astronomical phenomenon and a cultural event—one that brings ancient beliefs into direct conversation with modern life.

counterfactuals.output:
# India braces for rare, exceptionally long solar eclipse

**NEW DELHI** — Across India, millions of people are preparing to watch an unusually long total solar eclipse — while others plan to remain indoors, fast, pray or bathe in sacred rivers as centuries-old traditions collide with modern science.

The eclipse, expected to sweep across parts of India before moving over Asia and the Pacific, will be the longest total solar eclipse of the 21st century. At its maximum point, the moon will completely cover the sun for more than six minutes, though totality will last less time in most Indian locations.

Hotels and viewing sites along the path of totality are filling with astronomers, photographers and tourists. Travel companies are promoting special eclipse packages, while local officials in prime viewing areas are preparing for large crowds.

In the Hindu-majority nation, however, an eclipse is more than a celestial spectacle.

According to Hindu mythology, eclipses occur when the demon Rahu swallows the sun or moon. Although many Indians understand the astronomical explanation, traditional practices remain widespread. Some families avoid cooking or eating during an eclipse, cover food with basil leaves and clean their homes afterward.

Temples in several regions are expected to close during the event and reopen following purification rituals. Devotees are also traveling to sacred cities and pilgrimage sites, where bathing in rivers during or after an eclipse is believed by some to wash away sins and protect against harmful influences.

Authorities are preparing for especially large gatherings along the Ganges, including in Varanasi, one of Hinduism’s holiest cities. Other pilgrims are heading to religious centers such as Kurukshetra, where ritual bathing is traditionally associated with eclipses.

Superstitions have also fueled anxiety, particularly among pregnant women. Some have been advised by relatives not to go outdoors, use knives, sew, sleep or eat during the eclipse because of beliefs that the event could harm an unborn child.

Medical experts say there is no scientific evidence that eclipses endanger pregnancies. Their primary warning is far more practical: Looking directly at the sun without proper protection can permanently damage the retina.

Doctors and astronomers are urging people not to use sunglasses, exposed film, smoked glass, CDs or other improvised filters. Safe viewing requires certified eclipse glasses or indirect methods, such as pinhole projectors. Even when most of the sun is covered, the remaining light can cause serious eye injury.

Public health officials are also concerned about overcrowding and sanitation at pilgrimage sites, where large numbers of worshippers may enter rivers at the same time.

For India’s growing astronomy community, the eclipse offers a chance to counter misinformation and encourage scientific curiosity. Schools, science centers and amateur astronomy clubs are organizing supervised viewing events and distributing protective glasses.

Meanwhile, eclipse tourism is providing an economic boost. Visitors from India and abroad are booking hotels, buses and charter flights in hopes of finding clear skies. Some tour operators are combining observation trips with visits to temples and historic sites, marketing the event as both a scientific wonder and a cultural experience.

Weather remains the biggest uncertainty. Monsoon-season clouds could block the view in many areas, prompting some enthusiasts to travel long distances in search of clearer conditions.

Whether they greet the eclipse with telescopes, prayers or closed curtains, people across India are preparing for a brief period when daylight will fade, temperatures will drop and the sun’s corona will appear around the dark outline of the moon.

For scientists, it is a predictable alignment of the sun, moon and Earth. For many others, it is also a moment of spiritual significance — one that brings together faith, fear, celebration and awe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the cultural and commercial impact of the century’s longest total solar eclipse in India, using quotes from residents, doctors, astrologers, officials, and travel companies.
counterfactuals.output:
The 22 July 2009 eclipse—the longest total solar eclipse of the 21st century, with totality lasting up to 6 minutes 39 seconds globally—became in India both a mass religious event and a marketable spectacle.

### Cultural impact

Along the path of totality, especially in Varanasi, tens of thousands gathered before dawn to bathe in the Ganges and pray as the Sun disappeared. One pilgrim explained the religious motivation simply: **“I have come here to take a dip in the holy Ganges and pray to the sun god.”** Others treated the eclipse as an unusually auspicious moment for purification, despite Hindu traditions that also regard an eclipse itself as dangerous or polluting.

Those fears affected everyday life. Some families fasted, discarded food cooked before the eclipse, closed temples or kept pregnant women and children indoors. Residents described following instructions handed down by parents and grandparents: **“My mother-in-law has told me not to go out and not to eat anything during the eclipse,”** one expectant mother told reporters.

Astrologers amplified the anxiety. Indian astrologer Raj Kumar Sharma called the eclipse **“a bad omen for the whole world and India in particular,”** predicting that it could bring **“natural disasters like earthquakes, tsunamis and cyclones”** as well as political or communal conflict.

Doctors and science educators publicly challenged such claims. Physicians stressed that eclipses produce no special radiation capable of harming a fetus. As one doctor put it, **“There is no scientific evidence that an eclipse can harm an unborn child.”** The real medical risk, officials emphasized, was retinal injury from looking directly at the Sun without certified filters. Planetarium and government science officials therefore urged people to regard it as **“a rare celestial spectacle”**, while using eclipse glasses or indirect viewing methods.

### Commercial impact

The eclipse also generated a short-lived tourism economy. Hotels and guesthouses in viewing centers such as Varanasi, Patna and areas of Bihar and Gujarat advertised eclipse packages. Tour operators arranged riverfront viewing, scientific tours and trips intended for foreign “eclipse chasers.”

The most conspicuous product was a charter flight designed to rise above the monsoon clouds. Cox & Kings marketed seats on an aircraft flying at roughly 41,000 feet along the eclipse path; premium window seats reportedly cost about ₹79,000. A company representative said the response had been **“overwhelming,”** adding that **“the seats on the sun side have been sold out.”** Other seats were priced according to how good a view passengers would receive.

Thus, the eclipse exposed two Indias at once: one shaped by pilgrimage, inherited taboos and astrological warnings, and another presenting the event through astronomy, aviation and high-end tourism. Even heavy monsoon cloud—which spoiled the view in several places—did little to diminish its cultural or commercial significance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write an article explaining how scientific understanding, Hindu beliefs, and business opportunities intersect around a solar eclipse in India?
counterfactuals.output:
# When the Sun Disappears: Science, Hindu Traditions, and Commerce During a Solar Eclipse in India

A solar eclipse in India is more than an astronomical event. It can become a meeting point for scientific education, religious observance, tourism, media, and commerce. Although these spheres sometimes appear to conflict, they frequently coexist: a person may understand the mechanics of an eclipse, follow a family tradition connected with it, and purchase certified viewing glasses or travel to a location where the eclipse is visible.

## The scientific understanding

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, temporarily blocking some or all of the Sun’s light. In a **partial eclipse**, only part of the Sun is covered. During an **annular eclipse**, the Moon appears slightly smaller than the Sun, leaving a bright ring around it. A **total eclipse** occurs when the Moon completely covers the Sun for observers within a narrow path.

Indian scientific institutions, planetariums, universities, and amateur astronomy groups often use eclipses to promote public interest in astronomy. They may organize viewing sessions, explain orbital motion, or set up telescopes with suitable solar filters.

These efforts also address a serious safety issue: looking directly at the Sun can permanently damage the eyes. Except during the brief total phase of a total eclipse—and only for people located within the path of totality—the Sun must be viewed through properly certified eclipse glasses or specialized solar-viewing equipment. Ordinary sunglasses, smoked glass, exposed film, and homemade filters are not safe.

Simple indirect methods, such as a pinhole projector, allow people to observe the eclipse without looking at the Sun.

## Hindu beliefs and practices

Eclipses have a significant place in Hindu mythology and ritual life. One well-known account involves **Rahu**, who disguises himself to drink the nectar of immortality. After the Sun and Moon expose him, Vishnu severs his head. Rahu survives and is said to pursue and periodically swallow the Sun or Moon, producing eclipses. In some traditions, the related figure Ketu also plays a role.

This myth is not intended as a modern astronomical model. Rather, it belongs to a symbolic and religious framework through which communities have interpreted disruption, cosmic order, and renewal.

Practices vary greatly by region, family, sect, and individual belief. Some Hindus may:

- Fast before or during the eclipse  
- Avoid cooking or eating while it is underway  
- Chant prayers or mantras  
- Bathe after the eclipse  
- Visit a river, temple, or pilgrimage site  
- Make charitable donations  
- Place tulsi leaves in stored food  
- Observe additional precautions during pregnancy  

Others regard these customs as optional, symbolic, or outdated. Many people combine religious practice with full acceptance of the scientific explanation. It is therefore misleading to speak of a single “Hindu response” to an eclipse.

Temples also differ in their approach. Some close during the eclipse and conduct purification rituals afterward, while others organize prayers or remain open according to local custom.

## Where science and faith meet

Public discussion often presents science and religion as opposing forces: astronomers explain that no celestial being is swallowing the Sun, while religious authorities preserve inherited customs. In everyday Indian life, however, the relationship is usually more complicated.

Scientific understanding answers questions about physical cause, timing, visibility, and safety. Religious traditions may address meaning, identity, discipline, or community. One person can use an astronomical app to calculate the eclipse, wear certified viewing glasses, fast with family members, and donate to charity afterward without experiencing those actions as contradictory.

Eclipses can also encourage dialogue. Science centers may explain the difference between mythology and physical mechanism without mocking belief. Religious and community leaders can preserve ritual traditions while emphasizing safe viewing and rejecting harmful misinformation.

## Business opportunities around an eclipse

Because an eclipse creates intense but temporary public interest, it generates several kinds of commercial activity.

### Eclipse glasses and viewing equipment

Demand rises for certified solar viewers, telescope filters, binocular filters, and projection devices. Schools and employers may purchase glasses in bulk, while astronomy clubs may partner with reputable manufacturers.

This market also creates risks. Counterfeit or damaged glasses can cause eye injuries. Sellers should provide products that comply with recognized safety standards, source them from reliable manufacturers, and avoid making unsupported claims. Buyers should inspect viewers for scratches or punctures and follow guidance from scientific authorities.

### Tourism and hospitality

The eclipse’s path determines where it can be seen best. Towns with favorable visibility may attract photographers, astronomers, families, and international visitors. Hotels, transport companies, guides, restaurants, and local vendors can benefit.

Tour operators may offer packages combining eclipse viewing with visits to observatories, temples, heritage sites, or natural attractions. Responsible planning is essential: organizers should provide accurate weather and visibility information, safe equipment, crowd management, and realistic refund policies. No operator can guarantee clear skies.

### Religious travel and services

Pilgrimage centers—especially places associated with sacred rivers or major temples—may receive large numbers of visitors seeking ritual bathing, prayer, or post-eclipse ceremonies. This creates demand for transport, accommodation, food, sanitation, and offerings.

Commercialization can be sensitive in this context. Businesses should avoid exploiting fear, presenting paid rituals as scientifically necessary, or making promises that cannot be verified. Local authorities must also prepare for crowd safety, waste management, and pressure on waterways.

### Media, education, and digital products

Television networks and online platforms often provide live coverage, expert interviews, animations, and regional-language explanations. Educational publishers can create eclipse guides, classroom activities, and astronomy kits. Mobile apps can offer location-specific timings and alerts.

The strongest products distinguish clearly between calculation and prediction on one hand, and cultural interpretation on the other. Sensational claims may attract attention, but accurate and respectful coverage builds greater trust.

### Local enterprise

An eclipse can support small businesses as well as large companies. Local entrepreneurs may sell food outside fasting periods, provide transportation, host rooftop viewing sessions, produce commemorative crafts, or offer photography services. Municipalities can help by issuing temporary permits and ensuring that vendors follow safety and consumer-protection rules.

## A test of responsible communication

Eclipses are fertile ground for misinformation. Rumors may circulate about radiation, food contamination, pregnancy, earthquakes, or the need to buy particular remedies. Scientific evidence does not support claims that an eclipse produces special dangerous rays or causes food to become toxic. Normal food-safety practices remain relevant, but the eclipse itself does not poison meals.

Responsible businesses, media organizations, scientists, and religious leaders can all help separate personal observance from claims of physical danger. A family may choose not to eat for religious reasons, for example, without presenting the practice as a scientifically proven medical requirement.

## More than a shadow

In India, a solar eclipse illuminates as much as it darkens. It reveals how scientific literacy, inherited belief, public ritual, and market activity can occupy the same social space. The event can inspire curiosity about the solar system, renew cultural traditions, and create legitimate economic opportunities.

The most constructive approach neither dismisses religious participants nor permits tradition to be used as a cover for unsafe or deceptive claims. With accurate science, respect for diverse beliefs, proper eye protection, and ethical business practices, an eclipse can become a rare shared experience—one that connects the movements of the heavens with the complexities of life on Earth.

**Rare solar eclipse draws pilgrims and tourists across India and China**

**NEW DELHI, India (CNN)** — Millions of people across India and China are preparing to watch a rare total solar eclipse, as the moon’s shadow sweeps across some of Asia’s most densely populated regions.

For many, the event is more than a celestial spectacle. In the northern Indian city of Kurukshetra, authorities are preparing for vast crowds of Hindu pilgrims, who are expected to gather at sacred bathing sites and take part in prayers and purification rituals.

Sandeep Jaggi said traveling to Kurukshetra during an eclipse is a tradition his family has observed for generations. Like many devotees, the family believes bathing in the city’s holy waters during the eclipse carries special religious significance.

Astrologer R.K. Sharma said traditional Hindu beliefs associate eclipses with Rahu, a shadowy figure said to swallow the sun or moon. Some believers consider the period inauspicious and avoid eating, drinking or beginning important work until the eclipse has passed. Scientists, however, say an eclipse is simply the result of the moon moving between Earth and the sun.

The eclipse’s path will continue eastward into China, where large numbers of residents and visitors are expected to watch from cities along the route. Officials and astronomers are warning spectators not to look directly at the sun without approved protective glasses.

India’s travel industry is also turning the event into a tourism opportunity. Cox and Kings has organized a special flight to Gaya, offering passengers a chance to view the eclipse from above the clouds and avoid poor visibility on the ground.

Whether observed through protective lenses, from an aircraft or in the waters of Kurukshetra, the eclipse is bringing together science, tourism and centuries-old tradition across Asia.
